title: Pre-Rendered 3D Starship Game Prototype
description: Around 1993 I built a Turing-based starship game using hand-created 3DS4 models and a custom JAM asset system to simulate an interactive 3D bridge experience years before I had access to real-time 3D rendering. Pre-rendered ships, planets, targeting views, diagnostics, battles, navigation, and cinematic sequences were combined into a playable command interface. This project became the earliest recognizable ancestor of my later Bridge Captain games.

sections.title: Earliest Bridge Captain Prototype
paragraphs: This high-school project was effectively my first Bridge Captain-style game.
At the time I presented it as a Star Trek game, with the idea that the ships and branding could be changed later if I ever turned it into something commercial.

sections.title: 1993 Turing Game
paragraphs: I was introduced to Turing in 1992 and was building this starship project by approximately 1993.
I created the game myself and hand-built every 3D model used in my version.

sections.title: Pre-Rendered Interactive 3D
paragraphs: The project used pre-rendered 3D graphics as a substitute for real-time 3D.
Rather than treating the renders as passive artwork, I connected them to gameplay state so they behaved like interactive tactical, navigation, and diagnostic displays.

sections.title: Main Viewscreen
paragraphs: The main bridge viewscreen changed based on the current situation.
While in orbit, for example, a rendered planet rotated on the viewscreen.

sections.title: Targeting Camera
paragraphs: The targeting display used pre-rendered ship views to simulate a camera rotating around the selected enemy ship.
An animated targeting reticle zoomed into the selected part of the ship.
Changing targets changed the rendered ship orientation so the selected subsystem or area could be shown.

sections.title: Rotatable Damage Diagnostics
paragraphs: The diagnostics console displayed a pre-rendered Enterprise-D with visible areas of damage.
The ship could be rotated around any axis so damage could be inspected from different directions.

sections.title: Navigable Star Chart
paragraphs: The game included a navigable star chart used to move through the game world and select destinations.

sections.title: Turn-Based Starship Combat
paragraphs: Ships could appear on the tactical/viewscreen display and engage in turn-based combat.
The battle presentation used sequences of pre-rendered JAM assets rather than real-time polygon rendering.

sections.title: Combat Animation Sequences
paragraphs: Pre-rendered ship assets were used for multiple combat states and cinematic movements.
items: Enemy weapons firing toward the player's ship
Player weapons firing at the enemy

sections.title: Starbase Departure Sequence
paragraphs: The game began inside a starbase.
The bridge viewscreen showed the station bay doors opening and then played a pre-rendered sequence of the ship flying out into space.

sections.title: JAM Asset System
paragraphs: The project used my custom JAM asset-container system to organize graphics and animation frames.
Pre-rendered ships could be stored from multiple angles or as ordered animation sequences and selected by the game at runtime.

sections.title: Sprites and FMV
paragraphs: The rendering pipeline used several forms of pre-rendered presentation.
Some 3DS4 output became multi-angle sprite/JAM assets controlled interactively by the game, while longer sequences were treated more like FMV.

sections.title: All 3D Models Created by Me
paragraphs: Every 3D model used in my starship game was created by me in 3DS4.
The renders were then prepared for use inside the Turing/JAM game pipeline.

sections.title: Before Pre-Rendered Graphics Became Mainstream
paragraphs: This work was underway around 1993.
Donkey Kong Country arrived in 1994 and helped make pre-rendered 3D sprites highly visible in mainstream games.
At the time, my friend and I believed our use of pre-rendered 3D gave us a potential visual advantage.

sections.title: Parallel Work With a Friend
paragraphs: A friend and I were both experimenting with pre-rendered 3D game graphics, but we were building separate games.
I was developing this starship project while he pursued his own ideas.

sections.title: Commercial Ambition
paragraphs: We talked seriously about forming a game company after high school.
Our technical concern was less about whether we could build games and more about not knowing how to handle publishing, retail distribution, sales, and marketing.

By the time we finished high school, commercial games such as Donkey Kong Country and The 7th Guest had made similar pre-rendered presentation techniques much more visible, so we felt the visual advantage we had imagined was disappearing.

sections.title: Long-Term Design Lineage
paragraphs: The basic idea of commanding a starship through bridge consoles, navigation, tactical combat, targeting, and diagnostics continued through my later Bridge Captain projects.

historicalNotes: The legacy card was titled 'High School Pre-rendered Graphics'.
The legacy description states that Jamie and a friend experimented with 3DS4 pre-rendered graphics in high school roughly a year before Donkey Kong Country made the technique a major trend.
Jamie and his friend were building separate games rather than one shared project.
Jamie's game was a Turing-based Star Trek-style starship game and the earliest recognizable Bridge Captain precursor.
Jamie created every 3D model used in his game.
The pre-rendered assets were used directly in gameplay.
The main viewscreen could display animated orbital planets.
The targeting display simulated rotation around a Klingon ship and used an animated reticle that zoomed into the selected target area.
Changing targets selected different pre-rendered orientations/views.
The diagnostics display showed the Enterprise-D with damage information and allowed the rendered ship to be rotated around any axis for inspection.
The game included a navigable star chart.
The game included turn-based starship battles.
JAM animations depicted ships swooping into view, firing weapons, taking fire, and being destroyed.
The game began with a pre-rendered starbase departure sequence showing bay doors opening and the ship flying out.
Some rendered assets were multi-angle sprites/JAM sequences and others were FMV-style sequences.
Jamie was introduced to Turing in 1992 and was building this game by approximately 1993.
Donkey Kong Country released in 1994, providing a useful chronology anchor.
Jamie and his friend considered forming a game company but did not know how to solve publishing, sales, marketing, and retail distribution.
By the end of high school, mainstream commercial games had caught up substantially with pre-rendered visual techniques.

The surviving uploaded perrender_1.gif available in this conversation appears static to the assistant; animation behavior is therefore documented from Jamie's direct recollection rather than visual verification of that specific uploaded file.
